content: Black pepper, scientifically known as Piper nigrum, is a flowering vine belonging to the Piperaceae family. It is cultivated for its fruit, which is typically dried and used as a spice and seasoning. The same fruit is also processed to produce white pepper, red or pink pepper, and green pepper. Black pepper is native to South India and is extensively cultivated in tropical regions worldwide. The fruit, referred to as a peppercorn when dried, is a small drupe approximately five millimeters in diameter, dark red when fully mature, and contains a single seed. Dried and ground black pepper is one of the most commonly used spices in European cuisine and its culinary descendants. It has been valued since antiquity for both its flavor and medicinal properties. The characteristic spiciness of black pepper is attributed to the chemical compound piperine. Ground black peppercorn, often simply called pepper, is a staple on dining tables in many parts of the world, frequently paired with salt. The term pepper originates from the Sanskrit word pippali, which referred to long pepper. This term was adopted into Latin as piper, used by the Romans to describe both black and long pepper, as they mistakenly believed both spices came from the same plant. The English word pepper derives from the Old English pipor, which, in turn, traces back to the Latin term. The Latin root also influenced other languages, such as German (Pfeffer), French (poivre), and Dutch (peper). By the 16th century, the term pepper was also applied to the unrelated New World chile peppers. Figuratively, pepper came to mean spirit or energy as early as the 1840s, later shortened to pep in the early 20th century. Varieties of Pepper Black pepper is produced from the unripe green berries of the pepper plant. These berries are briefly cooked in hot water to clean them and prepare them for drying. The heat ruptures the cell walls of the fruit, accelerating the enzymatic browning process during drying. The berries are then dried in the sun or by machine for several days, during which the fruit around the seed shrinks and darkens, forming a thin, wrinkled black layer. Once dried, the fruits are called black peppercorns. White pepper consists solely of the seed, with the fruit layer removed. This is typically achieved by soaking fully ripe berries in water for about a week, during which the fruit's flesh softens and decomposes. The softened fruit is then rubbed off, leaving the bare seed, which is subsequently dried. Alternative methods involve mechanically removing the outer fruit layer from unripe black pepper berries. White pepper is often used in dishes like light-colored sauces or mashed potatoes, where the visibility of black pepper would be undesirable. There is some debate about whether white or black pepper is spicier, as their flavors differ due to the presence of certain compounds in the outer fruit layer of black pepper that are absent in white pepper. Green pepper, like black pepper, is made from unripe berries. Dried green peppercorns are treated to retain their green color, using methods such as sulfur dioxide treatment or freeze-drying. Pickled green peppercorns, also green, are unripe berries preserved in brine or vinegar. Fresh, unpreserved green pepper berries, which are largely unknown in the West, are used in some Asian cuisines, particularly Thai cuisine. Their flavor is described as piquant and fresh, with a bright aroma. However, they decay quickly if not dried or preserved. A rare product known as pink or red pepper consists of ripe red pepper berries preserved in brine and vinegar. Even more rarely, ripe red peppercorns can be dried using color-preserving techniques similar to those used for green pepper. Pink pepper from Piper nigrum is distinct from the more common dried pink peppercorns, which are the fruits of plants from a different family, such as the Peruvian pepper tree (Schinus molle) and the Brazilian pepper tree (Schinus terebinthifolius). In the past, there was debate about the safety of pink peppercorns, but this is no longer a significant concern. Sichuan peppercorn is another pepper that is botanically unrelated to black pepper. Peppercorns are often categorized by their region or port of origin. Two well-known types come from India's Malabar Coast: Malabar pepper and Tellicherry pepper. Tellicherry is a higher-grade pepper made from the largest, ripest 10% of berries from Malabar plants grown on Mount Tellicherry. Sarawak pepper is produced in the Malaysian portion of Borneo, and Lampong pepper comes from Indonesia's island of Sumatra. White Muntok pepper is another Indonesian product, originating from Bangka Island. The Pepper Plant The pepper plant is a perennial woody vine that grows up to four meters in height on supporting trees, poles, or trellises. It is a spreading vine that roots readily where trailing stems touch the ground. The leaves are alternate, entire, and measure five to ten centimeters in length and three to six centimeters in width. The flowers are small and produced on pendulous spikes four to eight centimeters long at the leaf nodes, with the spikes lengthening to seven to 15 centimeters as the fruit matures. Black pepper thrives in soil that is moist, well-drained, and rich in organic matter, avoiding conditions that are too dry or prone to flooding. The plants are propagated by cuttings about 40 to 50 centimeters long, tied to neighboring trees or climbing frames spaced about two meters apart. Trees with rough bark are preferred over those with smooth bark, as the pepper plants climb rough bark more readily. Competing plants are cleared away, leaving only enough trees to provide shade and allow free ventilation. The roots are covered in leaf mulch and manure, and the shoots are trimmed twice a year. On dry soils, young plants require watering every other day during the dry season for the first three years. The plants bear fruit from the fourth or fifth year and typically continue to bear fruit for seven years. The cuttings are usually cultivars selected for both yield and fruit quality. A single stem will bear 20 to 30 fruiting spikes. Harvesting begins as soon as one or two berries at the base of the spikes begin to turn red, before the fruit is fully mature but when it is full-grown and still hard. If allowed to ripen, the berries lose pungency and eventually fall off and are lost. The spikes are collected and spread out to dry in the sun, after which the peppercorns are stripped off the spikes. History Pepper has been used as a spice in India since prehistoric times. While it was grown in southern Thailand and Malaysia, its most important source was India, particularly the Malabar Coast in what is now the state of Kerala. Peppercorns were highly prized trade goods, often referred to as black gold and used as a form of commodity money. The term peppercorn rent still exists today. The ancient history of black pepper is often interlinked with, and confused with, that of long pepper, the dried fruit of the closely related Piper longum. The Romans knew of both and often referred to either as simply piper. It was not until the discovery of the New World and chile peppers that the popularity of long pepper entirely declined. Chile peppers, some of which when dried are similar in shape and taste to long pepper, were easier to grow in a variety of locations more convenient to Europe. Until well after the Middle Ages, virtually all the black pepper found in Europe, the Middle East, and North Africa came from India's Malabar region. By the 16th century, pepper was also being grown in Java, Sunda, Sumatra, Madagascar, Malaysia, and elsewhere in Southeast Asia, but these areas traded mainly with China or used the pepper locally. Ports in the Malabar area also served as stop-off points for much of the trade in other spices from farther east in the Indian Ocean. Black pepper, along with other spices from India and lands farther east, changed the course of world history. It was in part the preciousness of these spices that led to European efforts to find a sea route to India and consequently to the European colonial occupation of that country, as well as the European discovery and colonization of the Americas.
